prompt: What is a data race?

choices.text: Two tasks finishing in a different order on each run
choices.why: That is ordinary concurrency; lesson 14's group did it and was correct.

choices.text: Two threads touching the same memory at once, one of them writing
choices.why: Right: and the result depends on how their steps interleave.

choices.text: A task that never finishes
choices.why: That is a hang, not a race.

choices.text: An `async` call without `await`
choices.why: That is a compile error with a different message.

prompt: `Race.swift` printed 677275, then 800000 twice. What does the two right answers tell you?
hint: Section 02's worst thing about a race.

choices.text: The race fixed itself once the tasks warmed up
choices.why: Nothing changed; the interleaving happened to be harmless.

choices.text: The class is safe, and the first run hit a bug in Swift
choices.why: The class has an unprotected `var` written from several threads.

choices.text: Nothing: a racy program is right by luck
choices.why: Right: a passing run proves nothing about the next one.

choices.text: That eight tasks are too many for four cores
choices.why: The count of tasks is not the bug; the shared `var` is.

prompt: `minutes += m` looks like one step. How many steps is it, in section 02's account?
`swiftc` checks very little about concurrency unless you pass `-swift-version ___`.
What does an actor guarantee about its state?

choices.text: It is copied for each caller, like a struct
choices.why: An actor is a reference type; everybody holds the same one.

choices.text: Only its own code touches it, one call at a time
choices.why: Right: callers send requests and the actor runs them in turn.

choices.text: It can never change after `init`
choices.why: `minutes` changed 800,000 times a run.

choices.text: Its methods each run on a separate thread, reserved for the actor
choices.why: No thread is promised; one call at a time is.

prompt: From outside an actor, `week.minutes = 0`. What does the compiler say?
hint: Calls and writes are treated differently.

choices.text: Add `await` in front of it
choices.why: `await` fixes a call; a write from outside is refused whatever you write.

choices.text: Refused outright
choices.why: Right: ask the actor through a method such as `reset()`.

choices.text: Nothing; actor properties are public
choices.why: Isolation is not access control; lesson 17 is.

choices.text: A warning in Swift 6 mode
choices.why: It is an error.

prompt: Inside the actor's own `add`, `minutes += m` has no `await`. Why is none needed there?

choices.text: `+=` is a single machine step
choices.why: Section 02 showed it is three.

choices.text: Integers are `Sendable`
choices.why: True, and not the reason; the question is who is running.

choices.text: That code already runs on the actor
choices.why: Right: the `await` marks a crossing of the boundary, and there is none.

choices.text: The compiler skips checks inside methods of an `actor` type
choices.why: It checks them; there is simply nothing to cross.

prompt: In `Booking.swift`, both bookings passed `free >= 80` with 100 free. Why?
hint: What happens at an `await` inside an actor?

choices.text: A data race on `free`
choices.why: Every access to `free` happened on the actor, one at a time.

choices.text: Each call gave the actor up at its `await`, before subtracting
choices.why: Right: the second check ran in the gap the first left open.

choices.text: `guard` is not checked on actors
choices.why: It was checked, twice, and saw 100 both times.

choices.text: `async let` copies the actor
choices.why: Both calls reached the same actor; it is a reference.

prompt: Another call running on an actor while a first one is suspended at an `await` is called ___.
A cache actor checks `if cache[id] == nil`, then `await`s a download, then stores it. Two requests for the same id arrive together. What does section 04 predict?

choices.text: The actor runs the second request after the first finishes completely
choices.why: Only between awaits; the download is an await.

choices.text: A compile error in Swift 6 mode
choices.why: Booking.swift compiled in that mode; this is a logic bug.

choices.text: Both see nil and both download
choices.why: Right: the same shape as the double booking.

choices.text: A crash when the second store overwrites the first
choices.why: Overwriting a dictionary entry is legal; the waste is silent.

prompt: Put `Reserved.swift`'s `book` in the order its lines run.
Which of these is `Sendable` with nothing written?

choices.text: A `String` + `Int` struct
choices.why: Right: a value type of `Sendable` parts; it is copied when passed.

choices.text: A class with one `var note`
choices.why: Two holders could write the same object.

choices.text: A closure that captures a class instance
choices.why: That was exactly what `Sendables.swift` was refused for.

choices.text: A non-final class with only `let`s
choices.why: A class must also be `final` to declare it.

prompt: `Handover.swift` passes the same non-`Sendable` `Draft` into a detached task, and compiles. What changed from `Sendables.swift`?

choices.text: `Draft` became `final`
choices.why: It was `final` in both.

choices.text: The task is no longer detached
choices.why: Both programs use `Task.detached`.

choices.text: Nothing touches `draft` after it is sent
choices.why: Right: region-based isolation allows a real hand-over.

choices.text: It was compiled in Swift 5 mode
choices.why: Both were compiled with `-swift-version 6`.

prompt: `final class Course: Sendable { let name: String; var goal: Int }`. Why is it refused?

choices.text: A class can never be `Sendable`
choices.why: A final class of `let`s can.

choices.text: `goal` is a mutable stored property
choices.why: Right: shared and writable is what `Sendable` forbids in a class.

choices.text: `String` is not `Sendable`
choices.why: It is.

choices.text: A `Sendable` class needs an `init` with no parameters
choices.why: Any `init` will do.

prompt: A shared `Course` must change its goal while several tasks hold it. Which are sound designs? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Make `Course` an actor
choices.why: Yes: shared, changing state is what an actor is for.

choices.text: Make it a struct and send copies
choices.why: Yes: each task then has its own value.

choices.text: Mark it `@unchecked Sendable` and change `goal` freely
choices.why: No: that silences the check without protecting anything.

choices.text: Compile the module in Swift 5 mode
choices.why: No: the race stays, unreported.

prompt: Why are SwiftUI's views marked `@MainActor`?

choices.text: They run faster when every view is kept on the main thread
choices.why: Speed is not the reason.

choices.text: So that they are `Sendable`
choices.why: Isolation and `Sendable` are different promises.

choices.text: Only the main thread is allowed to touch the interface
choices.why: Right: and the compiler now holds code to that.

choices.text: Linux requires it
choices.why: SwiftUI is not on Linux at all.

prompt: In `Inherit.swift`, which task is refused for setting `screen.title`?

choices.text: Both
choices.why: The plain `Task` compiled.

choices.text: Only `Task.detached`
choices.why: Right: it inherits no actor, so it is nonisolated.

choices.text: Only the plain `Task`
choices.why: It inherits the main actor from `buttonTapped`.

choices.text: Neither, since `buttonTapped` is `@MainActor`
choices.why: A detached task does not run on the actor of its creator.

prompt: A screen update loads data for two seconds and then sets a label. Where should each part run?
hint: Section 06's shape of nearly every update.

choices.text: Both on the main actor, so that the order is clear
choices.why: Loading on the main actor holds up drawing for no reason.

choices.text: Both in a detached task
choices.why: Setting the label there is refused.

choices.text: The load away from it, the label on it
choices.why: Right: the main actor is free during the `await`.

choices.text: The label first, then the load
choices.why: The label needs what the load returns.

prompt: Match each way of compiling to the language mode it gets, unless told otherwise.
What does `.enableUpcomingFeature("ApproachableConcurrency")` in a fresh manifest do?

choices.text: Switches off the Swift 6 data-race checks
choices.why: A race is still an error with it.

choices.text: Adopts some planned defaults early
choices.why: Right: a bundle of upcoming features from Swift 6.2 that needs fewer annotations on one actor.

choices.text: Moves the target to Swift 5 mode
choices.why: That is `.swiftLanguageMode(.v5)`.

choices.text: Downloads a newer compiler for that target
choices.why: A manifest setting cannot change the toolchain.

prompt: A team moves a module to Swift 6 mode and gets forty concurrency errors. Which response matches this lesson?

choices.text: Mark every class `@unchecked Sendable` so it builds
choices.why: That stops the compiler looking, and the races stay.

choices.text: Read each one for what crosses and who else reaches it, and fix those
choices.why: Right: each error names a place a race can happen.

choices.text: Ignore them: a test suite that passes is proof enough
choices.why: `Race.swift` passed two runs of three.

choices.text: Wrap every method in `Task.detached`
choices.why: That removes isolation rather than adding it.

prompt: Match each tool to the problem it solves.

pairs.right: Shared state written by several tasks
